883.title: Nanda's festival in Gokula
883.hook: Vasudeva leaves his son beside sleeping Yashoda, and Gokula welcomes the baby with the birth rite
883.carry: samskara: sacred rites for life's passages
883.howItsDone: Hindus traditionally count sixteen samskaras, rites that mark a life from before birth to the funeral; the birth rite (jatakarma), the naming ceremony (namakarana) and a baby's first rice (annaprashana) are still kept by many families, and some communities keep Nandotsava, the day after Janmashtami, with curd and butter.

segments.voice: Yesterday the guards slept, the doors opened, Shesha's hoods sheltered father and child, and the river gave way. Your line was seva, serving the Lord in every form.

Gokula is silent. Vasudeva comes up out of the river, soaked, with the baby in his arms, and walks into the cowherd village where his friend Nanda lives. Nobody stops him. Nobody even stirs. The Bhagavata says everyone in Nanda's household is fast asleep. Inside, Nanda's wife Yashoda has just given birth too. She lies beside a newborn girl, so deeply asleep that she doesn't know what kind of child she has had.
screen: `GOKULA IS SILENT.` → `NANDA'S HOUSE ASLEEP.` → `YASHODA AND A NEWBORN GIRL.`

segments.voice: He makes the exchange. He lays his son beside Yashoda, picks up her daughter, and walks back across the river into the prison. He sets the girl on Devaki's bed. The text says he put the fetters back on his own feet, and the doors closed, as if nothing had happened. The rescue only works if he locks himself in again. And the girl he carries is no ordinary child: the Bhagavata has told us she is Yogamaya, the Lord's own power, born to Yashoda for this night. Now Gokula. Yashoda wakes up to a son, and Nanda is overjoyed. But the first thing he does isn't a party. He bathes, calls the priests, has the jatakarma done, the birth rite, and honors the gods and his ancestors. Then the party: he gives away cows and gifts, the village is swept and hung with garlands, and the cowherds splash each other with milk, curd and butter. Here's the teaching. Hindus mark the great passages of a life with sacred rites called samskaras, traditionally counted as sixteen, from before birth to the funeral. A new life isn't only a family's private joy. It's welcomed before God and the ancestors. That's why some communities keep Nandotsava, Nanda's festival, the day after Janmashtami, with curd and butter. And it's why, when a baby comes today, a grandmother may want a naming ceremony and a priest, not just a photo. She's doing what Nanda did.

884.title: the goddess in Kamsa's hands
884.hook: Kamsa grabs the eighth child, and she rises from his hands as the Goddess
884.carry: shakti: divine power, worshiped as the goddess
884.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Bhagavata honor the girl born to Yashoda as Yogamaya, a form of the Goddess; many devotees identify her with Vindhyavasini, the Goddess of the Vindhya hills, and many families keep both Janmashtami and Navaratri.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vasudeva left his son beside sleeping Yashoda and locked himself back in the prison, and Gokula welcomed the baby with the birth rite. Your line was samskara, sacred rites for life's passages.

A newborn cries in the cell. The guards jerk awake and run to the king. Kamsa leaps out of bed, the Bhagavata says, hair loose, stumbling, and rushes to the prison. This is the eighth child, the one the voice warned him about at the wedding. Devaki holds the baby close and begs him. It's a girl, a daughter of your own house. Don't kill a girl. You've taken so many of my children. Leave me just this one. Kamsa doesn't hear her. He tears the child out of her arms.
screen: `A CRY IN THE CELL.` → `KAMSA RUNS TO THE PRISON.` → `"IT'S A GIRL. LEAVE ME THIS ONE."`

segments.voice: He swings the baby by the feet to dash her against a stone, and she slips out of his grip. She rises into the air, and she is no longer a baby. The Bhagavata calls her the younger sister of Vishnu: a goddess with eight arms, holding weapons, in garlands and bright clothes. And she speaks down to him. What will you gain by killing me, fool? The one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Stop killing the helpless. Then she is gone. Kamsa frees Devaki and Vasudeva and even weeps, but by morning his ministers talk him into hunting newborns. He heard the truth, and chose fear. So who was she? The Bhagavata has already told us. Before the birth, Vishnu sent her, his own power, Yogamaya, and said people on earth would worship her under many names: Durga, Bhadrakali, Vaishnavi, Chandika, Ambika and more. Here is a big Hindu teaching hiding in a prison cell. Many Hindus call God's power shakti, and worship that power as the Goddess. The Lord and his shakti aren't rivals, and Krishna's story and Durga's aren't two separate worlds. The Devi Mahatmya, the Goddess's own great text, says it too: she would be born to Yashoda, in Nanda's house. That's why one family can keep Janmashtami in late summer and Navaratri in the fall, and bow to the same divine power in both: the power that protects, and that no tyrant can hold in his hands.

885.title: Putana, and why Krishna comes
885.hook: a lovely stranger brings poison to Nanda's house, and the baby she came to kill ends her
885.carry: an avatar comes to protect the good

885.howItsDone: The killing of Putana is told in the Bhagavata Purana's tenth book and is one of the childhood episodes Hindus retell in songs, dance-dramas and temple art; Hindus call each such coming of the Lord to earth an avatar.

segments.voice: Yesterday Yogamaya slipped from Kamsa's hands as the Goddess, the Lord's own power, and Kamsa chose fear and sent his people after newborns. Your line was shakti, divine power, worshiped as the Goddess.

Nanda is away in Mathura, paying his dues to the king, and Vasudeva, meeting him there, has warned him: go home quickly, there may be trouble in Gokula. Back in the village, a woman arrives. She is beautiful, the Bhagavata says, with flowers in her hair, a soft smile, a graceful walk. The cowherd women think a goddess has come to visit. She walks straight into Nanda's house, to the bed where the baby is lying.
screen: `NANDA IS AWAY.` → `A BEAUTIFUL STRANGER.` → `SHE WALKS TO THE BABY'S BED.`

segments.voice: Putana is one of Kamsa's killers. The Bhagavata calls her a demoness who goes from town to town killing infants, and today, by her magic, she has taken the form of a lovely woman. And the people guarding the child, Yashoda and Rohini, are so struck by her sweetness that they just stand there and watch her lift him. The danger doesn't break in. It's welcomed. Then the text turns the picture around: Putana takes the child on her lap the way someone picks up a sleeping snake, thinking it's a rope. As she comes near, the baby closes his eyes; the verse doesn't say why. She offers him her breast, smeared with poison. He feeds, and draws her very life out with it. She screams, let go, let go, and the earth shakes. As she dies, her disguise falls away, and her true body crashes down, crushing trees. On top of it, the cowherd women find the baby, playing, unafraid. Why does a baby god begin his life fighting demons? Krishna answers that himself, years later, in the Bhagavad Gita. Whenever dharma, the right order of things, falls apart, I come, age after age, to protect the good and to end the work of the wicked. Hindus call this coming down an avatar. Putana kills babies; the first thing the infant Krishna does is stop her. In Hindu teaching, that's what the Lord's coming is for: to stand with the ones who can't protect themselves.

886.title: the sweet smoke of Putana's pyre
886.hook: Putana's pyre smells sweet, and the narrator says even she reached a mother's place
886.carry: his grace answers even a poisoned offering
886.howItsDone: Vaishnava teachers and devotees retell Putana's story as an example of Krishna's grace, and the protective rites the cowherd women perform are described in the Bhagavata alongside the names of Vishnu they recite.

segments.voice: Yesterday Putana came smiling into Nanda's house with poison, and the baby, the avatar come to protect the good, drew her life out. Your line was an avatar comes to protect the good.

The cowherd women snatch the baby off Putana's body and carry him away, shaking. Then they protect him the way they know how. The Bhagavata describes it closely: they wave a cow's tail around him, wash him, mark his body with the dust of cows, and touch his limbs one by one while saying names of Vishnu, asking each name to guard a part of him. Feet. Knees. Belly. Heart. Then Yashoda nurses him to sleep. The danger is over. What the story does next with Putana is the surprise.
screen: `THE WOMEN TAKE THE BABY.` → `A NAME FOR EVERY LIMB.` → `YASHODA NURSES HIM TO SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Nanda comes home from Mathura with the other cowherds and finds a giant body lying across the village. He remembers Vasudeva's warning and is amazed: the man saw it coming. The cowherds cut up the body, pile it on a fire and burn it. And the smoke smells sweet, rising fragrant, the Bhagavata says, like aloe wood. Why would a child-killer's pyre smell like incense? The text gives its own answer: because the child had drunk her milk, her wrongs were burned away. Then the narrator, the sage Shuka, says something astonishing. Putana came to kill. She smeared poison on her breast and offered it to the Lord. Even so, because she offered him milk, she reached the place given to a mother. If even she, who came with murder in mind, was given that, Shuka asks, what of those who offer him love? That is the hinge. The Bhagavata doesn't dwell on punishing her. It dwells on the one thing she did that looked like a mother's act, and treats it as hers. Hindus call this kripa, the Lord's grace, and some Vaishnava teachers read Putana as its clearest picture: he answers the offering itself, and his touch transforms even an offering made in bad faith. So the same story holds both: the village's right to guard what it loves with every name it knows, and a mercy wider than anyone there expected.

887.title: the butter thief
887.hook: the village women bring Yashoda a long list of butter crimes, and can't stay angry
887.carry: lila: God comes close as a child at play
887.howItsDone: Krishna as the butter thief is a familiar figure in Hindu devotion: images of the child Krishna with butter in his hand are kept in homes and temples, many families offer him makhan mishri (butter with sugar) on Janmashtami and share it as prasad, and some communities hang pots of curd high up for teams to climb and break.

segments.voice: Yesterday Putana's pyre smelled sweet, and the narrator said even she reached a mother's place. Your line was his grace answers even a poisoned offering.

A group of women stands at Yashoda's door, and they have a list. They are the gopis, the cowherd women of the village. Putana is gone, and now there's a different problem, and he's a toddler. Butter has been disappearing all over the village. Curd too. Milk pots are broken. And every trail leads back to this house. So they come to his mother, half laughing, half fed up, and make their case, item by item.
screen: `WOMEN AT YASHODA'S DOOR.` → `BUTTER IS DISAPPEARING.` → `EVERY TRAIL LEADS HERE.`

segments.voice: Here is their list, as the Bhagavata Purana gives it. He turns the calves loose before milking time. He gets into the milk and curd, and when he's had his fill, he feeds the rest to the monkeys. If a monkey won't eat, he breaks the pot. People hang their pots high from the ceiling on ropes, so he drags over stools and a mortar and climbs, or makes a hole in the bottom of the pot and drinks from underneath. In a dark storeroom he doesn't even need a lamp: the jewels he wears light the way. Then the turn. All the while, Krishna sits beside his mother with wide, frightened eyes, the picture of a child who has never touched a pot. The women look at that face and can't keep scolding. They laugh. And Yashoda smiles and doesn't have the heart to punish him. Notice what kind of complaint this is. Nobody stops making butter. Nobody locks the door. They keep coming to report him, and in the reporting they get to talk about him and be near him. Hindus have a word for this side of God: lila, divine play. The Lord who holds the universe comes as a toddler with butter on his face, close enough to scold, to laugh at, to love. Some devotional teachers read the stolen butter as the devotee's heart, hung up high, that he finds his way into anyway. That's why, on Janmashtami, families set butter and sugar before baby Krishna: the thief gladly takes what's offered with love, and it comes back to them as prasad.

888.title: Damodara, tied by love
888.hook: Yashoda chases her son with a stick, and every rope she ties comes up two fingers short
888.carry: love is the only rope that holds God
888.howItsDone: Krishna bound by Yashoda's rope is remembered in his name Damodara, and some Vaishnava communities honor this story in the autumn month of Kartika with songs and lamps offered to Damodara.

segments.voice: Yesterday the gopis brought Yashoda their list, and the butter thief's frightened face stopped the scolding. Your line was lila, God comes close as a child at play.

Early morning in Nanda's house. The servants are busy elsewhere, and Yashoda is churning curd herself, pulling the rope back and forth around the churning stick, her bangles moving, singing, the text says, about the things her little boy has done. Then the little boy arrives. He's hungry, he wants his mother, and he takes hold of the churning stick so she can't go on. She lifts him into her lap and feeds him. A perfectly quiet scene. It's about to fall apart.
screen: `YASHODA CHURNING, SINGING.` → `HE GRABS THE CHURNING STICK.` → `A QUIET MORNING.`

segments.voice: On the fire, the milk starts to boil over. Yashoda sets Krishna down mid-meal and runs to it. He's furious. He bites his lip, cracks open the pot of curd with a stone, slips into another room and eats butter in secret. Yashoda comes back to a broken pot and no child. She finds him on an upturned mortar, handing butter from the hanging pot to a monkey. She picks up a stick. He jumps down and runs, and she runs after him. The Bhagavata pauses to marvel: the one the yogis can't reach even with their minds is being chased around the yard by his mother. She catches him. He cries and rubs his eyes. She drops the stick and decides to tie him to the mortar instead. The rope is too short, by two fingers' width. She adds another. Still two fingers short. Every rope in the house, always two fingers short, and the neighbor women laugh, and so does she. She's sweating now. Krishna sees how tired his mother is, and then, the text says, he lets himself be tied. The Bhagavata says this is what the scene shows: the Lord lets himself be held by those who love him. That's the heart of bhakti, devotion. Not power, not cleverness, not even the yogis' meditation. Love. Nothing in the universe can hold him; a tired mother's love can, because he allows it. Tradition says this is where one of his names comes from: Damodara, the one with a rope around his waist.
screen: `THE MILK BOILS OVER.` · `A BROKEN POT, A MONKEY, A STICK.` · `ALWAYS TWO FINGERS SHORT.` · then, large: `ONLY LOVE CAN HOLD HIM.`

segments.voice: People who love Damodara often light a small lamp before his image and sing to him. If you have a lamp or candle, light it; if not, picture one. Bring to mind someone who has tried very hard for you, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, and see them in the middle of that effort, a little tired. Say Damodara once, quietly. If you don't pray, simply thank that person in your heart.

889.title: the twin arjuna trees
889.hook: a boy drags his mortar between two old trees, and two cursed brothers step out free
889.carry: darshan: to see the Lord, and be seen
889.howItsDone: The freeing of Kubera's sons, called Yamalarjuna in Sanskrit, the twin arjuna trees, is retold in Krishna devotion as part of the Damodara story, and some images show the child pulling the mortar between two trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday every rope came up two fingers short, until Krishna let his tired mother tie him. Your line was love is the only rope that holds God.
screen: `THE BUTTER THIEF.` · `HE LETS HIMSELF BE TIED.`

segments.voice: So there he is, a small boy roped to a heavy wooden mortar, and his mother has gone back to her housework. A child might sulk, or cry. Krishna looks around the yard. Near the house stand two tall arjuna trees, side by side. And the Bhagavata lets us in on something nobody in the village knows: those two trees used to be people. They've been standing there a long time, waiting for this exact boy. Today the mortar goes for a walk.
screen: `TIED TO THE MORTAR.` → `TWO ARJUNA TREES.` → `THEY USED TO BE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The trees were once Nalakuvara and Manigriva, the sons of Kubera, the god of wealth. Proud and drunk, they were playing in a river with a crowd of young women, wearing nothing, when the sage Narada happened by. The women, embarrassed, covered themselves at once. The brothers didn't bother. So Narada cursed them to stand as trees, but his curse came with a way out: they would stand until they came before Krishna, and then be free. Now Krishna toddles toward them, dragging the mortar. He squeezes between the trunks. The mortar turns sideways and wedges against them. He pulls, and with a great crack both trees come crashing down. Out step two shining figures. They bow to the child, praise him, and ask that every part of them be his from now on: their words for his praise, their hands for his work, their eyes for seeing his holy ones. Then they go. The cowherds come running at the noise. The children playing nearby say: Krishna did it, dragging the mortar. The grown-ups can hardly believe it. Nanda unties his son, smiling. Here's the teaching. After ages as trees, what ended the curse was one thing: they came before him and saw him. Hindus call that seeing darshan. It's why people stand in long temple lines, especially at midnight on Janmashtami, for a few seconds before the deity. And in Hindu practice darshan goes both ways: you see the Lord, and the Lord sees you. One sight, and the brothers want even their eyes turned toward the holy from then on.
screen: `KUBERA'S SONS, PROUD AND DRUNK.` · `NARADA'S CURSE, WITH A WAY OUT.` · `THE MORTAR WEDGES BETWEEN THEM.` · then, large: `DARSHAN: TO SEE AND BE SEEN.`

segments.voice: If you have an image of Krishna, or of any deity, sit in front of it and simply look for a minute, without asking for anything: the eyes, the face, the hands. If you don't, look at something you find sacred, or at the sky. Let yourself be looked at, too. If you don't pray, just let the looking be slow and full.
